newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's BHP says assets dragging, could be sold.
newsitem.headline: Australia's BHP says assets dragging, could be sold.

text.p: Australia's biggest listed company, The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP), said on Monday about 10 percent of its global asset base was underperforming and that poor assets would be put up for sale if they did not improve.
The steel, mining and petroleum group's managing director, John Prescott, said that every asset was under the microscope.
"They've got to improve or they've got to go," Prescott told reporters after addressing a briefing seminar on the group.
In a frank assessment of the group's performance, Prescott and other executives told share analysts and fund managers that returns on capital and equity were inadequate.
Last Friday, BHP reported a 61-percent dive in net profit to A$410 million (US$264 million), its worst bottom-line result in a decade, after booking almost A$1 billion in one-off losses.
The losses stemmed mainly from BHP's decision to slice the value of underperforming assets, including a A$550 million write-down of its recently acquired U.S. copper operations.
"Returns being achieved currently are not acceptable," BHP's executive general manager for finance, Graeme McGregor, told the seminar.
In 12 months, the group's five divisions of steel, minerals, copper, petroleum and services would need to ensure their assets weare returning at least 10 percent return on capital.

"No established business or integrated business chain where more than one asset group is involved will be earning less than 10-percent return on capital or action will be taken to lift returns or the asset will be sold," McGregor said.
One share analyst has predicted BHP would sell assets of around A$1.5 billion in the current year ending May 31, 1998.
Analysts expect sales to centre on underperforming mining operations to centre on the minerals and copper divisions.
BHP has said it expects no more abnormal write-downs in 1997/98 and that it is confident the group would lift its financial performance substantially over the next three years.
But in part-recognition of BHP's increased exposure to the world copper price, the world's second biggest copper producer has adopted a new set of performance benchmarks for the group.
BHP confirmed on Monday it no longer insisted on achieving a 15-percent return on equity and instead aimed to be among the world's best 20 percent of companies in terms of returns to shareholders.

"The objective is to achieve a result that's comparable with what the best companies achieve and the best companies are taken from all companies, not just companies in our sector," managing director Prescott told the seminar.
"The purpose of abandoning the percentages (targets) is to recognise that there is volatility in our markets."

BHP also said it planned to lower its debt-to-equity ratios to around 30 percent from about 39 percent now, but it would keep investing in its future with A$4.5 billion in capital expenditure budgeted for 1997/98 alone.

But the group virtually ruled out for now another acquisition the size of its US$2.4 billion purchase of the Magma Copper Co last year. It said it could not do so without impairing its credit rating or seeking fresh equity funds.
"We want to ensure we retain our A rating," Prescott said.
